content: Discussion thread for #Project announcements > lean-mathlib-churn-bot
How does this compare with @Thomas Murrills's skimmer?

Neat! Seems like churnbot

  1. is written in python and only has access to textual log messages (this means that for instance it may not be able to fix identifier syntax properly when handling deprecations, since name resolution is complex and elaboration-sensitive, and suffix matching is not sufficient here)
  2. only applies specific try-this messages
  3. has a retry-on-failure loop (which skimmer only has planned)

Skimmer admittedly is nascent/WIP and currently can only apply try-this suggestions (scripts/runSkimmer.sh in mathlib, I should mention!). But it does apply arbitrary try-this suggestions of any form, due to interfacing with the actual lean elaboration process. I intend to return to skimmer and broaden its scope to the intended vision soon :) So, churnbot currently has more features what with repair, blame, and so on.

I'm also unwilling to use AI in skimmer except for helping me find, understand, and fix bugs, and/or writing code that I have an exact vision for.

Also, my future plans for skimmer look a bit different from churnbot—I'm interested in enabling more generic library-scale edits and in including "automated fixes" as a special case only for specific, predictable tasks—but overlap at least in the notion of applying edits deterministically and keeping the human in the loop when things can't be fixed deterministically. :) I like churnbot repair --interactive (I have a prototype of a similar thing for skimmer in unreleased work), the blame feature, and the zulip summary, that's neat! :)

This tool also has some overlap with hopscotch, especially the blame part. The other major part is the automated fixes -- hopscotch has an incipient fix subcommand that currently only works with deprecated modules, but the plan is to be able to compose with other "fixing" tools such as skimmer (or churn-bot for that matter).

It's great that this detects and handles a whole class of issues in a mechanical way. In my mind, however, it is valuable to fix issues 'one by one' (and this is the philosophy behind hopscotch and downstream-reports). Of course this is still possible by just focusing on a single 'bump', or pushing forward as long as all the fixes are 'mechanical' and stopping at the first one that churn-bot can't fix.

For example, the given https://github.com/FawadHa1der/FLT/pull/1 still places a lot of burden on a human maintainer by presenting 56 issues that must be 'fixed all at once' so the build passes, without attributing these to a particular 'offending' commit
